newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Canadian bond default could cost Belgian ASLK-CGER.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bond default could cost Belgian ASLK-CGER.

text.p: Belgian ASLK-CGER bank may have to pay its customers "a few hundred millions of francs" due to the 1994 default on subordinated bonds of Canadian insurer Confederation Life Insurance Co, which ASLK-CGER placed with its customers, the bank said on Thursday.

On Wednesday, a Belgian court ruled that ASLK-CGER and its Luxembourg unit Banque UCL had to pay customers the principal, interest and expenses relating to the bonds, because it had failed to warn customers about their subordinated status.
ASLK-CGER is 49.9 percent owned by Belgian-Dutch banking and insurance group Fortis.
UCL has since been renamed Fortis Bank Luxembourg.

"The court... only ruled that we should have mentioned the subordinated character of the issue," ASLK-CGER Chief Executive Officer Karel De Boeck said in reply to questions at the bank's 1996 earnings news conference.
De Boeck said that articles in the Belgian press which said the ruling could cost the bank up to 750 million francs were incorrect.
"We will determine our position in the coming weeks. We stand to lose a maximum of a few hundred million francs," De Boeck said.
The bank reported on Thursday that 1996 group net profit rose 25 percent to 6.82 billion francs.

The court case had been closely followed by the Belgian financial community, because it raises the question to what extent banks who sell eurobonds to customers can be held responsible for default of the issuer.

"When Confederation defaulted the investors just started looking for a way to attack the bank," an ASLK-CGER bank official told Reuters, adding that investors owning regular bonds had also lost their money and the subordinated bonds sold by ASLK did have a subordination clause on the security.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813, Fax +32 2 230 7710
